setting: a small‑scale solar installer in Malta weighing a community battery scheme (Sunlit Harbor)
prompt: I’m drafting a brief for our CFO, Maria, about a community battery project we’ve nicknamed “Sunlit Harbor.” The proposal is to install a 1.2 MW battery storage system on the roof of the East Harbour municipal building, funded by a mix of a €850,000 grant from the EU Green Malta fund, a €200,000 loan from our bank, and an assumed 30 % subsidy from the local council. That adds up to a total capital outlay of €1.05 M, which we say will be recouped in 12 months through reduced grid charges and a 15 % annual ROI from selling excess power to nearby residential blocks. We assume the municipality will adopt 20 % of the battery capacity within the first year and that the feed‑in tariff will stay at the current €0.12 kWh for at least three years—although we don’t actually know the tariff after 2025. The timeline is to sign the contract by 15 Oct 2024 and be operational by 1 Mar 2025. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to push this to Maria, list the three biggest ways the plan could fail (including any hidden cost or risk you spot), and specify the pre‑agreed trigger that would make us abort the project (e.g., if a certain metric isn’t met).

setting: a luxury yacht charter company in Monaco assessing a blockchain booking system (Azure Ledger)
prompt: I need your help stress‑testing a proposal I’m about to present to our CEO, Lucien Vale, about moving our charter booking platform to a blockchain ledger hosted on Azure. The plan calls for a $2.5 million development outlay, a 12 % transaction fee on each charter (currently 8 % on the legacy system), and we estimate a 3 % lift in bookings because high‑net‑worth clients will trust the immutable record. We assume the blockchain will cut fraud losses by roughly 50 %—our internal audit says we lose about $450 k a year to double‑booking and fake payments. The rollout is slated for Q3 2025, with a 24‑month pilot before full migration. The unknown is how long it will take for the European maritime regulator to approve blockchain‑based contracts; they have not given us a timeline. Please give me one clear recommendation, outline the main ways this could fail, and specify the pre‑agreed kill‑condition that would make us stop or pivot. The kill condition we discussed is if the pilot’s net ROI after 12 months is below 8 %. Also watch for any hidden assumptions—like the cost of integrating our existing CRM, which we have loosely quoted at $300 k but may be higher.

setting: a craft chocolate maker in Brussels weighing a fair‑trade cacao sourcing plan (Cocoa Tide)
prompt: I need a quick stress‑test of the fair‑trade cacao sourcing plan I’m about to present to our CEO, Lena Marquez. We currently spend €1.2 million a year on cocoa, buying 480 000 kg at €2.50 kg‑¹. The proposal is to shift 30 % of that volume (144 000 kg) to the new “Cocoa Tide” fair‑trade blend, which costs €0.45 kg‑¹ more but promises a 12 % price premium that we can pass to retailers. We’d start the pilot in Q3 2025, run it for 12 months, and if sales lift by at least 5 % we roll it out fully in 2026. I’m assuming the premium will be fully absorbed by our retail partners without affecting shelf price. The unknown is how much extra demand the ethical label will actually generate. Please give me: one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, the three biggest ways the plan could fail (including any hidden cost you see), and the specific result that would trigger us to kill the rollout (e.g., if net margin falls below X%). Note that we haven’t included insurance on the new shipments, and the cost‑benefit spreadsheet shows a €120 k profit increase—but the math adds the premium cost twice, so double‑check that. Thanks.

setting: a regional newspaper in Detroit evaluating a pay‑wall redesign (Inkforge Press)
prompt: I’m sending this to you because I need to brief Maya Patel, our chief revenue officer, next week on the pay‑wall redesign we’ve been testing with Inkforge Press. Right now we have 12,000 paid digital subscribers generating $1.6 million in annual revenue, and the new design is projected to cost $250,000 in development plus $35,000 for a three‑month pilot (Sept 1‑Nov 30, 2024). We assume a 30% conversion of the 40,000 monthly unique free visitors, which should lift subscriptions by roughly 1,800 and increase revenue by about $240,000. The plan also promises a 15% reduction in churn but we haven’t factored any extra customer‑support staffing (estimated $12,000) or potential legal review time. The biggest unknown is how our main competitor, MetroPulse, will respond—whether they’ll roll out a similar feature or launch a price war. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to push the redesign forward, list the three most plausible ways it could fail, and specify the pre‑agreed trigger that would make us stop or pivot (e.g., if pilot conversion falls below X%). Keep the answer concise and ready to hand over to Maya.

setting: a community theatre troupe in Wellington weighing a digital ticketing portal (Stage Ember)
prompt: Sam, Operations Manager, Kiwi Spotlight Theatre – we need your stress test before I pitch the Stage Ember digital ticketing portal to our Artistic Director, Maya Patel. Our current season runs 12 shows from 1 June 2025 to 15 August 2025, 3,500 seats total, average ticket price $120, and we spend $10,000 on paper prints and third‑party box office fees. Stage Ember charges a $2,500 one‑off setup, 2 % transaction fee, and we’re assuming an annual maintenance fee of $8,000. The contract says we’ll be live by 15 May 2025, giving us a two‑week test before the first performance. If the portal lifts ticket sales by 5 % we would add $90,000 in revenue, which I’ve calculated as roughly 15 % of our $600,000 seasonal budget. The unknown is how many of our patrons will actually switch to the app versus sticking with paper tickets; we have no data on adoption rates. I need one clear recommendation (go/no‑go), the three main ways this could fail, and the specific trigger—e.g., adoption below X % or cost overrun beyond $25,000—that would make us kill the project. Please keep the answer focused for Maya.

setting: a boutique IT consultancy in Dubai assessing a zero‑trust security framework (Cipher Oasis)
prompt: I need a quick stress‑test of the zero‑trust rollout I’m about to pitch to Fatima Al‑Mansoori, our CEO. We’ve allocated a $250,000 budget to implement Cipher Oasis across three pilot sites (the Dubai office, the Abu Dhabi data centre and the Riyadh remote‑work hub) over the next six months, starting 1 Oct 2026. The vendor says we’ll cut security incidents from our current 12 per month to under three, saving roughly $180,000 in breach‑avoidance costs (we’re assuming each incident costs $15,000 + overhead). We also assume our existing firewall can be decommissioned without a transition fee. The unknown is the licensing fee for the advanced analytics module, which the sales rep said “will be disclosed later.” I want you to give me: one clear recommendation on whether to move forward, the three biggest ways this plan could fail, and the specific trigger that would make us stop or pivot (e.g., if pilot‑site uptime drops below 98 % or if costs exceed 110 % of budget). Keep in mind that we haven’t accounted for staff training time or potential integration work with our legacy VPN, which might add hidden costs.

setting: a micro‑brewery in Portland, Oregon weighing a vegan beer line (Hop Lantern)
prompt: I’m the operations lead at Northwind Brewing and I need to brief our owner, Maya Patel, on the proposed vegan beer line, Hop Lantern. The plan calls for a $250,000 equipment purchase (brew kettles, a dedicated fermenter, and a plant‑based fining system) and a 9‑month rollout starting 15 Oct 2026. We estimate 1,200 barrels in year 1 at a wholesale price of $15 per barrel, which I’ve calculated as $20,400 in revenue (I’m assuming the price stays flat). Our current non‑vegan seasonal, Cedar Trail, cost $180,000 to launch and sold 1,500 barrels at $12 per barrel, yielding $18,000 in revenue. I’m assuming 15 % of Portland’s 300,000 craft‑beer consumers will switch to a vegan option within six months. The unknown is the distribution partner’s margin in the Pacific Northwest, which we haven’t secured. I need you to give Maya one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, outline the main ways this could fail (e.g., cost overruns, demand over‑estimation, regulatory labeling issues), and specify the pre‑agreed trigger that would make us kill the line (e.g., if quarterly sales fall below 200 barrels).

setting: a regional agricultural cooperative in Punjab evaluating a drone‑spray service (Golden Crop)
prompt: I’m preparing a brief for Mr. Harpreet Singh, our board chair, about hiring Golden Crop’s drone‑spray service for the upcoming wheat season. The proposal says three drones will operate from June 1 to September 30, each covering 60 ha per day, which would spray our 4,200 ha of acreage in 24 days. Golden Crop charges $120,000 upfront plus $40,000 per year for maintenance and software updates. We assume the drones will reduce pesticide usage by 15 % and labor costs by the equivalent of two full‑time spray operators ($48,000 each). The contract also includes a 5 % discount if we lock in a two‑year term by October 15, 2024. What I need back is: one clear recommendation on whether to proceed, the three most likely ways this plan could fail, and the specific metric that, if not met, would trigger us to cancel or renegotiate (for example, a cost per hectare exceeding a set threshold). Note that we still don’t know the exact downtime each drone will need for maintenance during the season, and the proposal seems to omit any fuel or insurance costs for the drones. Please keep the response focused on actionable insights for Mr. Singh.

setting: a corporate wellness startup in Stockholm considering a gamified health app (Vigor Loop)
prompt: I’m drafting a pitch for Lina, our CEO, and need the plan stress‑tested before our 15 May board meeting. We want to launch Vigor Loop, a gamified health app, in Q3 2025 with an initial marketing spend of $350 k, a development budget of $210 k, and an anticipated 12 000 active users by month 6. We assume we can negotiate a 15 % discount with the analytics vendor, which would bring their fee down from $75 k to $63 750. We also expect a churn rate of about 8 % per month and forecast $3.2 M in annual recurring revenue based on a $12 per month subscription. The unknown is the exact compliance cost for GDPR‑aligned data storage; the vendor gave us a range of $20–30 k but we haven’t locked it down. I need you to give Lina one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, outline the three biggest ways this rollout could fail, and specify the pre‑agreed trigger that would make us kill the project (e.g., if we miss a specific KPI). Keep in mind the arithmetic slip in the total cost calculation and the missing cost of user acquisition beyond the $350 k marketing spend. Please respond as if speaking directly to Lina.

setting: a heritage shoe manufacturer in Florence weighing a 3‑D‑printed sole initiative (Sole Artisan)
prompt: I need a quick stress‑test of the “Sole Artisan” 3‑D‑printed sole proposal before I take it to our CFO, Maria Rossi, next Thursday. We’ve run a pilot in March 2024 that produced 12,000 units at €4.20 each, versus the current leather‑cork sole cost of €5.00, which we say saves €0.80 per shoe. Our forecast assumes a 30 % increase in unit volume to 260,000 pairs in 2025, giving a total saving of €208,000, and we plan to invest €150,000 in a printer and €45,000 in training. The assumption is that customers will value the “made‑to‑order” story enough to sustain our current price point of €120 per pair. The real unknown is whether the polymer we’re testing meets the EU REACH safety standards and how long certification will take. I want you to give me one clear recommendation (go ahead, pause, or re‑design), list the three main ways this could fail (technical, market, regulatory), and specify the pre‑agreed trigger that would force us to kill the project—e.g., if the certification takes longer than six months or if the per‑pair cost exceeds €5.50. Please also flag any arithmetic or hidden cost issues you see.

setting: a small‑scale aquaculture farm in Vietnam weighing a vertical fish system (River Scale)
prompt: I’m drafting a brief for our CEO, Linh Tran, to get her sign‑off on converting our RiverScale vertical fish system at BlueWave Aquaculture into a fully automated operation. The current setup costs $152,000 (including tanks, pumps, and sensors) and produces 5,200 kg of pangasius per year, which we sell at $2.45 kg⁻¹, giving $12,740 in gross revenue. We estimate automation will add $48,000 in capital (robots, PLCs) and cut labor by 30 hours/month at $9 hour⁻¹, saving $3,240 annually. The assumption is that water temperature will remain between 24‑28 °C year‑round, keeping fish growth rates steady. We’ve heard that a competitor in the Mekong Delta achieved a 20 % yield increase with a similar system, but they also reported a 15 % rise in electricity use; we haven’t priced that electricity increase yet. I need you to prepare a concise response for Linh: one clear recommendation on whether to proceed, the main ways this plan could fail (including any hidden costs or market risks), and the specific result that would make us stop or pivot—e.g., if net profit after automation falls below $4,500 in the first 12 months. The unknown we can’t forecast is the market price for pangasius in Q4 2025. Please keep the response focused and actionable.

setting: a boutique perfume house in Paris assessing a personalized scent AI (Aroma Cipher)
prompt: I’m preparing a pitch for Céleste Dupont, co‑founder of Maison Lune, about launching Aroma Cipher, an AI that creates a custom perfume blend for each client after a 5‑minute questionnaire. We have a prototype that cost €45,000 to develop, and the vendor will charge €0.12 per inference. We expect to sell 12,000 bottles in the first year at €110 each, assuming a 30 % conversion from the 40,000 users we plan to reach through a June 1 launch campaign. The projected gross profit is €720,000, which we compare to the €500,000 profit we made last year from our bestseller “Midnight Rose.” The assumption is that the AI will not need additional data‑licensing fees beyond the initial €8,000. The unknown is how many customers will actually trust a machine‑generated scent over a perfumer’s recommendation. I need you to give Céleste one clear recommendation, outline the three biggest ways this rollout could fail, and state the specific result that would trigger us to halt the project. Thanks.

setting: a regional insurance broker in Oslo weighing a climate‑risk analytics platform (Frost Shield)
prompt: I’m the head of product at Nordic Risk Brokers, a regional insurance broker serving 400 corporate clients in Oslo and surrounding counties. We are evaluating a subscription to Frost Shield, a climate‑risk analytics platform that promises to reduce our underwriting loss ratio by 12% over the next 24 months. The vendor quotes a yearly fee of 1.8 million NOK and says implementation will take 6 weeks, after which we’ll need 2 full‑time analysts (each 850 k NOK per year) to operate it. We assume that the platform’s risk scores are 20 % more accurate than our current internal model, which we built in 2019 for 3.2 million NOK. The unknown is how much the new model will affect our premium pricing and whether the regulator will accept the outputs for compliance reporting. I need a recommendation for our CEO, Lena Berg, on whether to proceed, the three biggest ways the project could fail, and the specific trigger (e.g., if the first‑quarter loss‑reduction falls below 2 %) that would make us kill the plan. Also, point out any hidden cost or flaw in our calculations.

setting: a community garden collective in Nairobi evaluating a rain‑water harvesting network (Green Tide)
prompt: Hi, I need you to stress‑test the rain‑water harvesting network proposal I'm taking to Ms. Amani, our Board Chair. Green Tide would install 12 200‑liter tanks across our three garden plots (Plot A 0.8 ha, Plot B 0.5 ha, Plot C 0.3 ha). We estimate each tank yields 1250 L per month, so total capture 15 000 L/month, enough for 80 % of irrigation needs (we currently use 19 000 L/month). The capital cost is $12 000, with an $8 000 grant secured; we plan to cover the remaining $4 000 from the collective’s reserve of $5 000. Installation is slated for 15 Sep 2024 to 30 Oct 2024, with commissioning by 1 Mar 2025. I’m assuming the average monthly rainfall will stay at 110 mm, as recorded in 2022‑23, and that the community will maintain the system without extra labor costs. The unknown is the annual maintenance fee—manufacturer quotes range $400‑$900. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, list the three biggest ways this could fail, and tell me the specific result (e.g., capture <60 % of projected volume for two consecutive months) that would trigger us to stop or redesign the network.

setting: a specialty cheese coop in Normandy weighing a nationwide tasting tour (Curd Voyage)
prompt: I need you to stress‑test my Curd Voyage proposal before I present it to Lucien Moreau, the co‑op’s board chair. The plan is to launch a 12‑stop tasting tour across France from 1 June 2025 to 30 August 2025, visiting 12 cities. We budget $150,000 total, allocating $12,500 per stop for venue hire, logistics and staff, and we expect 5,000 visitors overall, averaging about 420 per stop. Our forecasted revenue is $180,000 from ticket sales at €30 each, giving a 10 % margin after we deduct the $150 k cost plus an assumed $8,000 marketing fee. The assumption is that each host venue will provide free space and utilities. The unknown is the exact licensing fee for serving small‑batch cheese paired with wine in each region—we have only a rough estimate of €200 per location. I need one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, the three most likely ways the plan could fail, and the specific result that would trigger us to kill the tour (for example, if ticket sales fall below a certain threshold).

setting: a regional renewable energy fund in Johannesburg weighing a battery‑storage acquisition (Solar Crest)
prompt: I’m preparing to pitch the acquisition of Solar Crest’s 200 MWh battery‑storage portfolio to Ms. Lerato Mthembu, our fund’s chair. The deal price is $85 million, with an expected annual revenue of $12 million and a projected IRR of 9 % using a discount rate of 8 %. We’d need an additional $5 million for integration and expect $1.2 million per year for maintenance. The acquisition is slated to close in Q4 2025, and the performance guarantee runs through 2030. I’m assuming electricity prices will rise 4 % annually, which drives the revenue forecast, but the upcoming government storage tax credit is still unknown. The battery life is estimated at 10 years, and we’ve factored in a 5 % degradation per year. I’m also comparing this to a $70 million green‑hydrogen project we evaluated last year, but I may have missed the grid interconnection upgrade cost of roughly $3 million that would be required for Solar Crest. Please give me one recommendation on whether to proceed, identify the main ways this could fail, and state the specific result that would trigger us to kill the plan (e.g., capacity factor falling below a certain threshold).

setting: a boutique legal tech startup in Copenhagen assessing a contract‑automation SaaS (Clause Loom)
prompt:
I’m drafting a proposal to present to our COO, Lina Sørensen, about moving from our current in‑house contract builder to Clause Loom’s contract‑automation SaaS. We’ve been paying €120 k per year for the legacy system, handling roughly 12 000 contracts annually (≈€10 per contract). Clause Loom quotes €9 per contract, plus a fixed €15 k integration fee and a €5 k annual support add‑on. We estimate we can cut processing time by 30% and lower per‑contract cost to €8, which would yield a net saving of €240 k over the next 12 months. The rollout would start on 1 Nov 2025, with a 4‑week integration phase and a 3‑month pilot ending 31 Jan 2026. 

Our key assumption is that churn will stay at 5% and that the 30% time reduction translates directly into a cost saving. We haven’t priced the potential need for custom API development (unknown) nor the impact of Clause Loom’s rate‑limit throttling on peak loads. I need you to give Lina one clear recommendation, outline the three biggest ways this switch could fail, and state the specific result (e.g., pilot cost exceeding €30 k over budget) that would trigger us to kill the plan or revisit it.

setting: a heritage textile mill in Manchester weighing a sustainable dyeing process (Thread Ember)
prompt: Olivia, Operations Manager at Manchester Loomworks, here. I need a concise briefing for Dr. Eleanor Finch, our Chief Sustainability Officer, on whether to move forward with the Thread Ember sustainable dyeing process. We have a $2.5 million budget approved for a pilot that would run from 1 June to 31 August 2024 on Line 3, processing 150 kilograms of fabric per day. The vendor guarantees a 45 % water reduction versus our current 1.2 million‑dollar annual water bill—that would save roughly $600 k (they’re assuming 45 % of $1.2 M equals $600 k, which I haven’t double‑checked). They also say cycle time will increase by 12 %, which we estimate will cut throughput by about 200 hours per month, potentially costing $120 k in lost labor. I’m assuming we can retrofit the existing vats in two weeks with no production loss. The unknown is the long‑term durability impact on color fastness after 30 washes, which the vendor hasn’t tested yet. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to present this to Dr. Finch, list the three main ways the pilot could fail (technical, financial, regulatory), and specify the pre‑agreed kill condition – i.e., the result that would make us stop or change course.

setting: a small‑scale biotech lab in Buenos Aires evaluating a CRISPR‑based crop improvement program (Gene Harvest)
prompt:
I’m preparing a briefing for Dr. Lucía Marquez, our CEO, about launching Gene Harvest, our CRISPR‑based program to improve soy yield in the Pampas. The plan calls for a $2.1 million R&D spend over 18 months starting Q3 2025, plus a $350 k regulatory filing fee, so we’re budgeting $2.45 million total (I’ve added a $100 k contingency that I think covers everything). We’ll run field trials on 5,000 ha, aiming for a 12 % yield lift (from 3.2 t/ha to 3.6 t/ha) and anticipate fertilizer savings of $0.15 per kg. The regulatory deadline is 31 Dec 2026, with the first commercial harvest slated for March 2027.  

I’m assuming the edited trait will not introgress into wild relatives, and that the Argentine authority will view our CRISPR edits the same way they treated the conventional breeding project that cost $1.9 M and took five years. The real unknown is the probability of regulatory approval—nothing in the dossier quantifies that risk. I need you to give me one clear recommendation on whether to push ahead, the main ways this could fail (technical, regulatory, economic), and the specific result that would trigger us to stop or re‑plan the project.

setting: a boutique coffee roaster in Colombia assessing a direct‑to‑consumer subscription service (CopperMoor Roasters)
prompt:
Sofia,

I’m preparing a proposal to launch a direct‑to‑consumer subscription for CopperMoor Roasters and need it stress‑tested before I present it to you next week. We plan to start on 1 June 2025 with an initial marketing spend of $120 k, aiming for 2,500 active subscribers by month 3, each paying $30 per month. Our cost per bag is $12 and we estimate $5 shipping per order, so the unit margin is $13. We’re assuming a churn rate of 8 % per month and that 70 % of our existing retail customers will stay on the wholesale channel rather than switch to the subscription. The break‑even point should be hit in month 6, after which we forecast a net profit of about $250 k in the first year.

What I need from you is a single recommendation on whether we should move forward, the three most likely ways this plan could fail, and the specific metric that, if it materialises, would trigger us to kill the program or pivot. The unknown that worries me most is the actual shipping cost for customers in remote Andean regions, which we haven’t been able to price yet. Thanks.

setting: a midsize biotech firm in Sweden evaluating a CRISPR‑based crop improvement program (NordicGene Labs)
prompt: I’m preparing a briefing for CEO Anders on the CRISPR‑based wheat improvement program we’ve been developing at NordicGene Labs. The proposal calls for a three‑year investment of 12 million SEK per year, with the expectation that we can boost average yields by 15 % in the target regions of southern Sweden. Our market analysis shows a potential revenue pool of roughly 200 million SEK over the next five years if we capture 5 % of the national wheat market. We assume the EU regulatory authority will grant us full approval within 24 months, based on the 18‑month timeline we observed for a similar trait in corn. The nearest competitor, GreenField Agro, claims a 10 % yield lift using conventional breeding, and they spent about 8 million SEK on R&D, which we’re using as a benchmark. An unknown at this point is the field‑trial variance we’ll see across the 12 test sites; early data from the first two sites show a 9 % increase, but the rest are still pending. I need you to give me one clear recommendation for Anders, outline the three biggest ways this plan could fail, and tell me the specific result that would trigger us to stop or pivot the project.

setting: a small family‑owned vineyard in New Zealand weighing a virtual wine‑tasting platform (SilkGrove Estates)
prompt: I’m drafting a pitch for Ethan Cheng, the founder of SilkGrove Estates, and I need the plan stress‑tested before I present it next Thursday, 2024‑10‑24. The virtual wine‑tasting platform we’re evaluating costs $27,000 upfront plus $1,800 per month, and the vendor promises a 9 % lift in online sales in the first 12 months, assuming our conversion rate matches our website’s current 4 %. The unknown is the churn rate of users after their first virtual tasting and how many will convert to repeat purchases. setting: a municipal water utility in Canada reviewing a smart‑meter rollout (MaplePond Waterworks)

We intend to replace 12,000 residential meters with the new AquaSense devices, at a quoted hardware price of $375 each, which we’ve calculated as a total cost of $5.4 M. The full deployment is slated to start 1 Jul 2025 and finish by 31 Dec 2026; we’re assuming the meters will integrate seamlessly with our existing SCADA system, which hasn’t been tested under sub‑zero temperatures. I need you to give Maya one clear recommendation on whether to proceed, outline the three biggest ways this could fail (including any hidden costs or risks we haven’t priced), and tell me what specific result—such as a 30 % higher than expected installation cost or a cybersecurity breach—should trigger us to stop or rethink the project.

setting: a fast‑growing e‑learning startup in Kenya planning an AI‑driven tutoring chatbot (BrainNest Edu)

setting: a regional airline in the Philippines considering a loyalty‑points partnership (SkyHarbor Airways)
prompt: I’m the commercial lead at SkyHarbor Airways and need to stress‑test a loyalty‑points partnership I’m taking to our CEO, Maria Santos, next week. The idea is to partner with Pacific Retail Group, which has 2 million members, and give them 1 point per Philippine peso spent on tickets. I’m assuming Pacific’s members will value airline points as much as they value retail points, but we have no data on how many of those 2 million members will actually sign up for SkyHarbor’s program. Also, we’re comparing this to a competitor’s similar deal that cost $800 k and generated a 10 % revenue lift, even though their average ticket price was $95. Please give me one clear recommendation, outline the main ways the plan could fail, and tell me what specific result would trigger us to kill or pause the partnership.

setting: a heritage furniture maker in Italy exploring a circular‑design subscription (OliveArc Studios)
prompt: I need a quick stress‑test of the circular‑design subscription we plan to pitch to Marco Bianchi, co‑founder and CEO of OliveArc Studios. We’re targeting 1,500 active subscriptions in the first 12 months, each paying €120 per month, which we’ve projected will generate roughly €2.2 million in revenue (1,500 × 12 × 120). The refurbishing cost per returned piece is €30, and we expect an average churn of 8 % per quarter.
